$comment: Job handlers that cannot run. Read by scripts/check-job-producers.mjs.
Two shapes. `kind` alone means nothing anywhere enqueues it. `kind` plus `root` means
the implementation named by `root` registers it and only the other implementation
produces it, so the handler is dead in that half of the codebase.
A ratchet, not a mute button: a row whose handler has gained a producer, or been
deleted, fails the check with the line to remove. It can only shrink. It already has —
expire_invites and purge_trash were here as dead everywhere, and PR #23 seeded all four
recurring kinds in the Postgres root, so those rows are gone and what is left is the
narrower fact that the in-memory root still schedules nothing.
purge_trash and expire_invites are gone from here too now: MemoryJobs grew the same
scheduleRecurring the Postgres root already had, seeded with the same kinds and
intervals, so both are produced on the in-memory root as well. purge_documents is
untouched and stays -- nothing scheduled it there.
Prose in these rows is the reason a future reader trusts the exemption, so it has to be
checkable. An earlier version of the expire_invites row claimed the sweep was called
from the account-jobs timer in apps/rest with a `.catch(() => 0)`. That call never
existed: runAccountJobs touches exports and deletions, and the `.catch(() => 0)` there
belongs to exports.expireOld, which is a different port. Two agents grepped for the
invite version independently and neither found it. Corrected below, and worth stating
as a rule: cite a line someone can open.

known.why: packages/services-memory/src/index.ts registers it; only the Postgres root seeds it. Unlike the trash there is no timer standing in, so on the in-memory path an expired document is never purged at all. That path loses everything on restart regardless, which is why this is recorded rather than urgent — and it is also the path the review calls the one failure that is both silent and total, so it should not be relied on either way.
